transcript.text: Shutdown & Short-Run Loss Minimization
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-31
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply Shutdown & Short-Run Loss Minimization.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A firm should operate in the short run when price covers average variable cost, even if price is below average total cost. A lump-sum tax acts like fixed cost. AVC represents avoidable cost in the short run. Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Find the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output where marginal revenue equals rising marginal cost.
At that output, compare price with average variable cost.
Operate in the short run when price covers average variable cost; shut down when price falls below it.
A firm may operate at a loss when it covers variable cost and contributes something toward fixed cost.
WATCH OUT

Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating. A fixed-cost change affects profit and ATC but not MC or AVC, so it does not change the marginal output choice or shutdown threshold.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHUT DOWN OR OPERATE?

Cost / revenue is vertical; Firm quantity is horizontal. The price line is $10, below minimum AVC of $20 at point A, quantity 22, so the firm shuts down. Points B, C and D lie farther up the rising marginal-cost curve; C is at about quantity 44 and minimum ATC $41.

The horizontal price line is $10, below minimum AVC of $20 at point A. At every positive output, revenue per unit would be less than avoidable variable cost. The firm minimizes its short-run loss by shutting down and paying only fixed cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
P is below minimum AVC. What should the firm do?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Monopoly Demand, Revenue & Marginal Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-37
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Interpret Monopoly Demand, Revenue & Marginal Revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A monopolist faces the market demand curve, so selling another unit requires a lower price and makes marginal revenue (MR) less than price. A price taker sells each unit at the same price; a monopolist lowers price to expand output. Price taking removes the price effect that drives monopoly MR below price.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Start with the monopolist's downward-sloping market demand curve.
Because selling another unit requires a lower price, marginal revenue lies below demand.
For a linear demand curve, marginal revenue shares the vertical intercept and falls twice as quickly.
Marginal revenue is positive where demand is elastic and negative where demand is inelastic.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to equate MR and price. Linear MR shares demand’s vertical intercept and is twice as steep. For a downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WHY MR FALLS BELOW PRICE

Price / cost ($) is vertical; Quantity is horizontal. MR crosses MC at quantity 40 and $20. Demand gives price $40 at that quantity; ATC is $45. The demand-MC intersection near quantity 67 and $27 is not the monopoly output choice.

At 40 units, the demand curve shows a price of $40, while the marginal-revenue curve shows MR of $20. Total revenue is $40 x 40 = $1,600. The gap between price and marginal revenue illustrates why a monopolist's MR lies below demand when lowering price is necessary to sell another unit.
CHECK YOURSELF
For a single-price monopolist, which curve gives price at each output?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Market Structure & Product Differentiation
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-43
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Identify Market Structure & Product Differentiation.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Monopolistic competition combines many sellers and relatively easy entry with differentiated products. Differentiation gives each firm a downward-sloping demand curve and some pricing discretion. Close substitutes limit that discretion; entry can eliminate economic profit in the long run.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A market has many sellers and easy entry.
A dental practice competes mainly through evening hours, online scheduling, and unusually fast appointments.
A restaurant has many nearby rivals, but customers value its menu and atmosphere enough that a small price increase does not drive everyone away.
A market has many small sellers and easy entry, but every seller offers exactly the same product.
A neighborhood café competes through atmosphere, menu, and location.
WATCH OUT
Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING PRODUCT DIFFERENTIATION

A city has many coffee shops, entry is relatively easy, and each shop offers a distinct menu and atmosphere. Because customers view the shops as close but imperfect substitutes, each shop faces downward-sloping demand and has limited price-setting power. Those facts identify monopolistic competition.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is a differentiated firm’s demand downward sloping?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Product Variety, Efficiency & Model Limits
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-47
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate Product Variety, Efficiency & Model Limits.
Difficulty: Advanced
THE CORE IDEA

Product differentiation provides variety that consumers value, but firms may produce below the quantity that minimizes average total cost. Assess the benefit of a better product match alongside higher unit costs and markups. Productive efficiency alone does not measure the full welfare effect of variety.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
More varieties can better match different preferences.
Smaller production runs can raise average cost.
Compare the value of variety with costs and markups before judging welfare.
WATCH OUT
Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WEIGHING THE VALUE OF VARIETY

Two bakeries offer different breads. A neighborhood values having both varieties, but dividing sales between the bakeries can leave each producing below its lowest-cost scale. More variety can therefore benefit buyers while raising cost per loaf. A welfare judgment weighs those benefits against the extra resource cost; a markup alone does not measure the value of variety.
CHECK YOURSELF
A town gains more fitness-class options, but each provider serves fewer customers at a higher average cost. What benefit and cost should be compared?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-48
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Oligopoly is a market in which a few large firms account for much of sales and must anticipate rivals' responses. Concentration describes the distribution of market shares. It can signal strategic interdependence, but market definition, entry, and actual conduct also matter.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a market dominated by a few firms with meaningful barriers to entry.
Each firm's price, output, or advertising decision depends on how rivals are expected to respond.
Use concentration measures as evidence about structure, not as a complete verdict about competition.
The defining clue is strategic interdependence among the important firms.
WATCH OUT
Do not use firm count alone. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING MARKET CONCENTRATION

Horizontal axis: Firm or fringe, with categories A, B, C, D and Other; vertical axis: Market share in percent. The five bars have printed values A 38 percent, B 32 percent, C 12 percent, D 9 percent, and Other 9 percent. Other is a separate aggregate category, not labeled as a single firm.

Firms A and B hold 38% and 32%, together 70% of sales. Firms A through D hold 91%; the remaining 9% is a fringe of smaller firms. A large firm considering a price cut must anticipate how its major rivals will respond.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why does the 9% Other category not necessarily represent one large rival?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Game Theory Foundations: Payoff Matrices, Best Responses & Nash Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-49
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibrium.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Game theory represents strategic choices with players, actions, and payoffs that depend on what others do. Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the players, each player's available actions, and the payoff associated with every action combination.
For each possible rival action, mark the action that gives a player the highest payoff.
A dominant strategy is best regardless of the rival's action.
A Nash equilibrium is a cell where every player's action is a best response to the others.
WATCH OUT
A cell with the largest combined payoff need not be an equilibrium. Check each player's incentive to switch while holding the other player's action fixed.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING A NASH EQUILIBRIUM

For each rival strategy, identify the action with the larger payoff. If column X is chosen, row A gives 9 rather than 3 from row B. If column Y is chosen, row A gives 2 rather than 1 from row B. Thus, A is the row player's strictly dominant strategy. For the column player, X gives 9 rather than 3 when row A is chosen, and 2 rather than 1 when row B is chosen. Thus, X is the column player's strictly dominant strategy. Because A and X are mutual best responses, (A, X) is the unique Nash equilibrium.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why must payoff order be stated?
READY?

Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-28
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine money-market equilibrium and interest-rate adjustment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Money-market equilibrium occurs where the quantity of money supplied equals the quantity demanded at a particular interest rate. With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes the interest rate up. Liquidity preference theory explains the interest rate as the price that balances money supply and money demand.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
At a fixed money supply, greater money demand raises the equilibrium interest rate.
Higher income or prices can increase money demand for transactions.
A lower interest rate raises the quantity of money demanded along the existing curve.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve. At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING THE MONEY-MARKET RATE

Nominal interest rate (%) is vertical; Quantity of money is horizontal. Vertical money supply rises from MS0 at 100 to MS1 at 125. With downward money demand unchanged, the nominal interest rate falls from 4% to 2%.

Money supply increases from 100 to 125 while the money-demand curve is unchanged. The added 25 units move equilibrium down the demand curve, lowering the nominal interest rate from 4% to 2%. The graph therefore illustrates how an expansionary money-supply change reduces the short-term interest rate.
CHECK YOURSELF
At the current interest rate, households want to hold more money than the fixed money supply provides. Which adjustment moves the market toward equilibrium?
READY?
